(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

- driver-boundary-guard: Specialized reviewer for values that cross a DRIVER boundary — anything DataQ receives from a database connector, pyiceberg, pandas/pyarrow, or a cloud SDK and then type-narrows (isinstance / dtype checks / hasattr). Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>

<example>

Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". # Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

{"body":"Implementation slice of **ADR 0032 — email OTP sign-in** (see the umbrella issue for the full picture).

## Scope — backend core

1. **`sessions` table** — modeled on `api_keys` (ADR 0026): `dq_sess_` opaque token, ~256-bit, SHA-256 hex at rest (verifier secret — deliberately NOT in the SecretStore), fixed expiry (default 24h, no refresh pair), owner FK `ondelete=CASCADE`, revoked_at for logout.
2. **`otp_codes` storage** — hashed code (SHA-256 is fine: the protection is caps, not KDF — a 6-digit code has ~20 bits), 10-min TTL, single-use, max 5 verify attempts per code, re-request invalidates outstanding codes, constant-time compare.
3. **Endpoints** (unauthenticated, standard error envelope):
   - `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` — accepts an email; **uniform response whether or not the email is signup-eligible** (anti-enumeration); sends the code synchronously (SMTP timeout ~5s, real errors surfaced as 502-class, never silently swallowed).
   - `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/verify` — email + code → sets the session cookie (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax) and returns the user shape.
   - `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` — revokes the session, clears the cookie.
4. **Auth seam branch** — `get_current_user` resolves, in order: `dq_live_` bearer (PAT) → `dq_sess_` session cookie → Azure JWT (when configured). Same uniform-401 discipline as PATs. `/mcp` is an explicit **non-goal**: sessions are a browser credential; PATs remain the headless/MCP credential.
5. **Config block `AUTH_EMAIL_*`** — separate from alerting's `EMAIL_*` (a rate-limited/misconfigured alert mailer must never block sign-in): `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST/PORT/USERNAME/FROM/PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME` (password resolved via `SecretStore` by name, same pattern as the alert mailer), plus `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (signup gating — see the identity issue).
6. **Fail-closed startup** — extend the `init_auth` contract: `otp` mode with incomplete `AUTH_EMAIL_*` or an empty signup allowlist → refuse to boot, naming the missing vars. A deployment must never come up half-authenticated.

## Hard dependency

- **#725 (rate limiting), auth-endpoint slice, lands with or before this.** `otp/request` is the app's first unauthenticated mail-sending endpoint: per-email and per-IP limits are load-bearing security controls here, not hygiene.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Sessions + OTP models/migrations (additive, backward-compatible; up+down tested)
- [ ] Three endpoints with the adversarial battery (bad/expired/reused codes, attempt-cap lockout, enumeration probes return uniform responses, NUL/oversize inputs)

1	# ADR 0032 — Email OTP sign-in: a passwordless third authenticator behind the `get_current_user` seam
2	
3	- **Status:** Accepted
4	- **Date:** 2026-07-09
5	- **Deciders:** @TheurgicDuke771
6	- **Amends:** ADR [0026](0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md) — Decision 6 answers its deferred phase-2 question "migration path for `users.aad_object_id` → generic principal" for the email slice; ADR [0028](0028-cloud-neutral-image-runtime-config-generic-oidc.md) — the frontend `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` enum gains `otp` and the SPA gains a cookie credential beside the OIDC bearer flow.
7	- **Related:** ADR 0026 (PATs — the verifier-secret and seam pattern this copies; Basic auth rejected there stays rejected), [0010](0010-provider-agnostic-infrastructure-seams.md)/[0013](0013-marketplace-distribution-and-anti-lock-in.md) (portability guardrails)
8	- **Issue:** umbrella [#738](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/738) → slices #734 (backend) · #735 (identity) · #736 (frontend) · #737 (SMTP pre-flight); hard prerequisite #725 (rate limiting, auth slice). Ratified 2026-07-09 — slices unblocked.
9	
10	> **Amendment (2026-07-09, [ADR 0033](0033-workspace-roles-rbac.md)):** the OTP
11	> signup contract gains **`AUTH_OTP_DEFAULT_ROLE`** (default `member`) — the
12	> workspace role assigned at self-signup; the `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`
13	> write-through **wins over the default** for bootstrap admins. Decision 6's trust
14	> statement also widens: with in-app-promotable stored admins, mailbox compromise
15	> of **any admin-role holder** is admin compromise — not only allowlisted
16	> addresses.
17	
18	## Context
19	
20	Human sign-in today has exactly one real path: Azure AD (`fastapi-azure-auth` on the backend, generic OIDC against Azure on the frontend). PATs (ADR 0026) are headless-only and need an existing user to mint them; dev-bypass is single-user local eval. So a BYOL customer on a non-Azure cloud, and the post-wind-down local-first posture (#591), have **no way to log a human in**. ADR 0026 rejected HTTP Basic because it would make DataQ a password system (storage/hashing policy, lockout, reset flows). Email OTP is passwordless — proof of mailbox ownership is the credential — so it closes the gap without reopening that rejection. It **complements, not replaces**, the generic OIDC/JWKS backend validator (ADR 0013 Phase 2, tracked in #732): generic OIDC serves customers with an IdP; OTP serves small teams without one.
21	
22	The trade this makes explicit: OTP swaps "bring an IdP" for **"bring a mailbox"** — an org SMTP relay is an install prerequisite of this mode. A deployment with neither uses `bypass` (solo/eval, unchanged). And unlike Basic auth, OTP still makes DataQ an identity *issuer* for its users: enumeration, mail-flooding, and code-guessing become our attack surface to own — hence the hard caps and the #725 dependency below.
23	
24	## Decision
25	
26	1. **Third authenticator behind the existing seam.** `get_current_user` resolves, in order: `dq_live_` bearer (PAT) → **`dq_sess_` session cookie** → Azure JWT. Same uniform-401 discipline. `/mcp` is a **non-goal**: sessions are a browser credential; PATs remain the headless/MCP credential.
27	2. **Auth-mode ladder, fail-closed — realized by two coordinated contracts.** The ladder is `bypass` (solo/eval, nothing required) · `otp` (small team — bring SMTP) · `oidc` (org IdP). Mode selection is split across components today and stays split: the **frontend** `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` runtime enum (ADR 0028 — nginx-injected, never read by the backend) gains `otp`; the **backend**, which currently infers its mode from `AZURE_*`/`AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` in `init_auth`, gains OTP selection via the presence of the `AUTH_EMAIL_*` + allowlist block — #734 owns keeping the two selectors coordinated and documented together. Extending the `init_auth` fail-closed contract: OTP configured incompletely (partial `AUTH_EMAIL_*` **or an empty signup allowlist**) refuses to boot, naming the missing vars — never a deployment that looks up but can't log anyone in.
28	3. **Sessions copy the PAT mechanism, not the PAT table.** Opaque `dq_sess_` token, SHA-256 at rest in a new `sessions` table (verifier secret — never in the SecretStore), fixed expiry (default 24 h), **no refresh pair** — re-running OTP is the "refresh". Expiry and revocation are **enforced at the seam** (an expired or logged-out session is a uniform 401 on the next request — verified by tests, not just stored columns). Delivered as an **HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie** riding the same-origin nginx proxy (ADR 0028 §5), so the SPA never holds the token (no JS-readable storage). CSRF stance: Lax blocks cross-site POSTs, which only holds if **every cookie-authenticated mutation is POST-only** — that invariant plus login-CSRF on verify/logout are explicit test obligations (#734/#736). DataQ does not self-issue JWTs — no signing-key lifecycle to own.
29	4. **OTP mechanics sized to its entropy.** A 6-digit code is ~20 bits, so the protection is caps, not KDF: 10-min TTL, single-use, max 5 verify attempts, re-request invalidates prior codes, constant-time compare, SHA-256 at rest. The request endpoint returns a **uniform response whether or not the email is eligible** (anti-enumeration) and sends nothing for ineligible addresses.
30	5. **Signup gating is mandatory — no open registration.** `otp` mode requires `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` and/or `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`. First-admin bootstrap: the operator puts their own address in the signup allowlist and `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`, then signs in to their own mailbox — no seeded password to rotate.
31	6. **One user row per normalized email (identity linking).** `users.aad_object_id` becomes nullable with a unique index on `lower(email)` (two-step migration + duplicate-email audit first — #735). An OTP sign-in whose email matches an existing AAD-provisioned row resolves to **that row**: mailbox proof is the credential, and in a single-tenant AAD the email claim is tenant-controlled, so the join is trustworthy. Grants, shares, and PATs never fragment across authenticators. Consequence to state plainly: **email is the root of trust** — mailbox compromise is account compromise (and admin compromise if that address is on `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`).
32	7. **The OTP mailer is its own config block, on the request path.** `AUTH_EMAIL_*` (host/port/username/from/password-secret-name — password via `SecretStore`, same pattern as alerting) is separate from alerting's `EMAIL_*`, reusing the SMTP+STARTTLS code shape but **not** the publisher: the alert path treats mail as best-effort (the mailer no-ops when unconfigured and the composite publisher isolates its send errors so a flaky mailer can't fail a run); OTP send is the opposite contract — synchronous (~5 s timeout) on the request path, with send errors surfaced to the caller, never isolated away. A misconfigured alert channel can never block sign-in, and vice versa. An admin-gated **SMTP pre-flight** ("send me a test mail", #737) surfaces misconfiguration at install time.
33	8. **Hard prerequisite: #725's auth-endpoint slice.** `otp/request` is the app's first unauthenticated mail-sending endpoint; per-email and per-IP rate limits land with or before it.
34	
35	## Consequences
36	
37	**Positive** — a real human sign-in for non-Azure and fully-local deployments (the local-first posture's missing auth mode); no password store, ever; bootstrap without seeded credentials; all four moving parts copy proven in-repo patterns (PAT verifier storage, `init_auth` fail-closed, SecretStore-by-name, runtime frontend config), so the implementation risk concentrates in the one genuinely new thing — the identity migration (#735).
38	
39	**Negative / accepted** — a mailbox becomes an install prerequisite of `otp` mode (mitigated: `bypass` remains for the mailbox-less solo case, and the BYOL audience has SMTP by definition); DataQ takes on identity-issuer abuse surface (mitigated by caps + gating + #725, but it is new surface); email-as-root-of-trust is a real trust-model shift that the security docs must state; the `users` migration touches every authz path and needs the two-step discipline; sessions add a second browser credential model (cookie) beside the OIDC bearer flow.
40	
41	## Alternatives considered
42	
43	- **HTTP Basic / passwords** — rejected in ADR 0026; unchanged.
44	- **Magic links instead of codes** — rejected: corporate mail scanners prefetch URLs (consuming single-use links), links leak into logs/referrers, and codes copy across devices. Same transport, worse failure modes.
45	- **TOTP authenticator apps** — rejected for this gap: enrollment needs a retrievable shared secret (password-adjacent storage) plus a recovery story — heavier than the problem. Fine as a *future* second factor on top.
46	- **Self-issued JWT sessions** — rejected: buys statelessness we don't need at this scale, costs a signing-key rotation story; opaque hashed tokens match the PAT precedent and are trivially revocable.
47	- **Bundle the generic OIDC validator instead** — rejected as *instead* (different audience: IdP-owning orgs vs IdP-less teams); it remains the marketplace prerequisite in #732 and arrives on its own track.
48	- **Open signup (no allowlist)** — rejected: DataQ holds failing-row samples (PII); self-provisioning by anyone who can receive email is unacceptable as a default.

- **Bundle the generic OIDC validator instead** — rejected as *instead* (different audience: IdP-owning orgs vs IdP-less teams); it remains the marketplace prerequisite in #732 and arrives on its own track.
- **Open signup (no allowlist)** — rejected: DataQ holds failing-row samples (PII); self-provisioning by anyone who can receive email is unacceptable as a default.

content.content:
=== #735 ===
feat(auth): OTP identity model — users email-unique migration (two-step), linking rule, signup gating (ADR 0032)

Implementation slice of **ADR 0032 — email OTP sign-in** (see the umbrella issue). This is the risky half — it touches the identity model every authz decision hangs off.

## Scope — users identity migration + linking rule + signup gating

Today `users.aad_object_id` is `nullable=False, unique=True` and **`email` has no unique constraint** (`backend/app/db/models.py:115-116`); `_upsert_user` conflicts on `aad_object_id` only. OTP users have no AAD identity, so:

1. **Data audit first**: verify no duplicate (normalized) emails exist in any live DB before adding the unique index (dev-bypass/demo/seed users are the likely collisions).
2. **Two-step migration** (working agreement — backward-compatible only):
   - Step 1: add nullable-`aad_object_id` support + a unique index on `lower(email)`; deploy.
   - Step 2: code that upserts OTP users by email ships after the migration is live.
3. **Identity linking rule (decided in ADR 0032): one user row per normalized email.** An OTP sign-in whose email matches an existing AAD-provisioned row resolves to **that row** (mailbox proof is the credential; in a single-tenant AAD the email claim is tenant-controlled, so the join is trustworthy). Never two rows for one human — suite grants, shares, and PATs must not fragment across authenticators.
4. **Signup gating is mandatory — no open registration.** `otp` mode requires a non-empty `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` and/or `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`; a request for a non-eligible email sends nothing and returns the same uniform response (anti-enumeration + anti-mail-bombing). First-admin bootstrap = operator puts their own email in both the signup allowlist and `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`.
5. **Document the trust consequence**: under OTP, mailbox compromise = account compromise (and workspace-admin compromise if the mailbox is on `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`). Email is the root of trust; deployments mixing `otp` and `oidc` must understand the linking rule implies it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Email-uniqueness audit documented (and a cleanup path if collisions exist)
- [ ] Two-step migration shipped in order, up+down tested, rollback plan in the PR
- [ ] Linking behavior covered by tests: OTP→existing-AAD-row resolves to same user id; grants/PATs intact
- [ ] Gating tests: non-allowlisted email → no mail sent, uniform response; empty allowlist → boot refusal (with the backend-core issue)
- [ ] `docs/security.md` + deployment docs describe the email-as-root-of-trust model

=== #736 ===
feat(auth): OTP frontend — DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp, two-step sign-in UI, cookie session handling (ADR 0032)

Implementation slice of **ADR 0032 — email OTP sign-in** (see the umbrella issue).

## Scope — frontend `otp` auth mode + sign-in UI

`DATAQ_AUTH_MODE` is currently `'bypass' | 'oidc'` (`frontend/src/auth/config.ts:30`), injected at runtime via the ADR 0028 nginx envsubst contract. Add the third mode:

1. **Runtime config**: `DATAQ_AUTH_MODE=otp` through `window.__DATAQ_CONFIG__`; fail-closed like the existing modes (unknown/incomplete config → the unconfigured error screen, never a silent bypass).
2. **Sign-in flow**: two-step screen — email entry → code entry (with resend + cooldown UX, attempt-cap error states, and the uniform "if this address is eligible, a code was sent" copy mirroring the backend's anti-enumeration response).
3. **Credential handling**: the session is an **HttpOnly cookie** set by `otp/verify` — the SPA never sees or stores the token (no localStorage/sessionStorage). API calls ride the cookie through the same-origin nginx proxy; `AuthGate` treats a 401 as signed-out and routes to the sign-in screen; logout calls `POST /auth/logout`.
4. **`useMe`/`MeProvider`** works unchanged (cookie auth is transparent to `/me`); verify the admin-nav gating and profile page render for an OTP user.
5. **E2E**: Playwright specs for the happy path, wrong-code, expired-code, **expired/revoked-session → 401 → sign-in redirect** (session invalidated server-side mid-session, next navigation lands on sign-in), and signed-out redirect (OTP mode can run fully local — no Azure needed — so this can join the standard CI E2E lane with a mailhog/smtp4dev container or a test-mode code hook; pick the approach that doesn't weaken prod code paths).

<result>## Research Summary — Email OTP Backend Infrastructure (#734)

I've mapped the five key areas for the email OTP implementation. Here are the exact locations and findings:

---

### 1. **Alerting Email Publisher (SMTP+STARTTLS Shape)**

**File:** `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/alerting/email.py`

**SMTP+STARTTLS Implementation (lines 373–382):**
- `_send()` method uses `ssl.create_default_context()` + `smtplib.SMTP(…, timeout=15.0)` → `server.starttls()` → `server.login()` → `server.send_message()`
- **Timeout:** `_SMTP_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 15.0` (line 34) — best-effort no-op on failures
- **Password resolution (lines 283–286, 315–318, 343–346):** Calls `self._secret_store.get(self._password_secret_name)`, catches `SecretNotFoundError` and logs warning, then returns early (quiet no-op)
- **Error handling:** Composite layer isolates send errors so a flaky mailer doesn't fail runs (line 264)
- **Settings read:** Expects `username`, `password_secret_name`, `sender`, `recipients`, `smtp_host`, `smtp_port` as constructor args (lines 238–257)

**Key pattern for OTP reuse:** The `_send()` method is the reusable code shape (SMTP+STARTTLS transport); the error handling must **differ** — OTP surfaces errors on the request path (synchronous, ~5s timeout per ADR 0032 §7), not isolated like the alert publisher.

---

### 2. **Settings Class (Pydantic Settings)**

**File:** `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/core/config.py`

**Email alerting settings (lines 346–356):**
```python
email_smtp_host: str = "smtp.gmail.com"
email_smtp_port: int = 587
email_username: str | None = None
email_from: str | None = None
email_to: str = ""  # comma-separated recipients
email_password_secret_name: str | None = None
```

**Settings class structure:**
- **Lines 25–36:** `SettingsConfigDict` with:
  - `env_file=".env.app"` — reads `.env.app` only (not root `.env`)
  - **`extra="forbid"`** (line 34) — typos/stale keys crash startup (the enforcement mechanism)
  - `case_sensitive=False` — env vars auto-normalized to lowercase
  
**Boot-time validator pattern (lines 426–487):**
- `@model_validator(mode="after")` method `_validate_secret_store()` (line 426)
- Validates OpenBao/Azure/Redis config **at startup** before first use
- Raises `ValueError` naming missing/invalid fields (examples: lines 460–462, 467–472, 478, 481, 484)
- **Precedent for fail-closed AUTH_EMAIL_* validation:** Reject incomplete config at startup, naming which vars are missing

**`*_SECRET_NAME` indirection pattern:**
- Lines 309–318: `adf_webhook_secret_name`, `airflow_webhook_secret_name`, `dbt_webhook_secret_name` — all stored as STRING names, resolved via `SecretStore.get()` at runtime
- Password values NEVER embedded; `SecretStore` resolves them by name (line 283: `self._secret_store.get(self._password_secret_name)`)

---

### 3. **SecretStore Seam (Interface + Error Types)**

**File:** `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/backend/app/core/secrets.py`

**Protocol interface (lines 188–200):**
```python
@runtime_checkable
class SecretStore(Protocol):
    def get(self, name: str) -> str: ...
    def set(self, name: str, value: str) -> None: ...
    def delete(self, name: str) -> None: ...  # fail-soft, idempotent
```

**Exception types (ADR 0039 decision 6 — lines 111–138):**
- **`SecretNotFoundError`** (lines 111–118): Raised ONLY when the secret genuinely is not set. Callers treat this as a legitimate state ("no webhook configured", "run without extra credential").
  
- **`SecretStoreUnavailableError`** (lines 121–137): Raised when the store couldn't answer (dead token 403, sealed vault 503/5xx, missing KV mount, transport error, non-JSON 200, KV v1 envelope). **Deliberately NOT a subclass** — the type is load-bearing. Example from lines 129–131 shows why: if vault outage folded into `SecretNotFoundError`, alerts would skip silently, connections would run without credentials, and the operator would see "not configured" during an outage.

**Usage pattern in email publisher (lines 283–286):**
```python
try:
    password = self._secret_store.get(self._password_secret_name)
except SecretNotFoundError:
    log.warning("email_password_unresolved", secret_name=self._password_secret_name)
    return
```
This is **best-effort**, no-op on either exception type.

**For OTP (per ADR 0032 §7):** Must use the same `get()` call but surface errors to the caller (synchronous contract), not suppress them.

---

### 4. **Env-Var Reference Documentation**

**Primary file:** `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.env.app.example`
- This is the **complete, annotated** env-var reference (lines 1–266)
- Every Settings key is documented here with comments explaining purpose, format, defaults

**Deployment guide:** `/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/deploy/README.md`
- **Lines 25–56:** Production prerequisites table (the "What you must change" checklist)
  - `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` (line 31)
  - `AZURE_*` settings (line 32)
  - `SECRET_STORE` (line 34)
  - Alerting settings not explicitly tabulated, but referenced via #416/#837
  - NOTE: No `AUTH_EMAIL_*` or `AUTH_OTP_*` documented yet — this is the gap #734 fills

**Format pattern observed:**
- `.env.app.example` has every key with inline comments (purpose, format, examples)
- `deploy/README.md` prerequisites table summarizes production-critical settings
- New `AUTH_EMAIL_*` and `AUTH_OTP_*` vars should appear in **both places**

---

### 5. **Existing AUTH_* Settings Names (Provider-Neutral Contract)**

**Currently in config (lines 38–194 of config.py):**
- `AZURE_TENANT_ID`, `AZURE_API_CLIENT_ID`, `AZURE_SPA_CLIENT_ID` (lines 182–185) — Azure-specific
- `AZURE_ALLOW_GUEST_USERS` (line 193) — Azure-specific
- `AUTH_DEV_BYPASS` (line 195) — **provider-neutral**, dev-only auth bypass

**No existing `AUTH_EMAIL_*` or `AUTH_OTP_*` yet.** ADR 0032 §2 and §7 specify the names that **will be introduced**:

**From ADR 0032:**
- **`AUTH_EMAIL_*`** block (§7, line 32 of ADR):
  - `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_HOST`, `AUTH_EMAIL_SMTP_PORT`, `AUTH_EMAIL_USERNAME`, `AUTH_EMAIL_FROM`, `AUTH_EMAIL_PASSWORD_SECRET_NAME`
  - (Same coordinate names as alerting's `EMAIL_*`, but separate config block for OTP)
  
- **`AUTH_OTP_*`** block (§5 & §10 of ADR):
  - `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` (signup allowlist, required)
  - `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (signup allowlist, required)
  - `AUTH_OTP_DEFAULT_ROLE` (amendment, default `member`)

**Pattern precedent:** These mirror the **provider-neutral `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS`** contract (config.py line 265) — not bound to Azure, usable in any deployment (bypass / otp / oidc modes per ADR 0032 §2).

---

### Key Takeaways for Issue #734

1. **SMTP code shape is in `/alerting/email.py` lines 373–382** — reuse `_send()` method for OTP, but route errors differently (surface vs. isolate).

2. **Settings validation precedent:** Bootstrap validator at lines 426–487 of `config.py` — fail-closed, naming missing fields. Apply the same pattern to `AUTH_EMAIL_*` + allowlist validation.

3. **SecretStore exception types are load-bearing** — never conflate `SecretNotFoundError` (state) and `SecretStoreUnavailableError` (outage). ADR 0039 decision 6 is the reference.

4. **New env vars belong in two places:**
   - `.env.app.example` (annotated, all keys)
   - `deploy/README.md` prerequisites table (production-critical ones)

5. **No `AUTH_*` names yet exist** — the OTP implementation will introduce the first user-facing `AUTH_EMAIL_*` and `AUTH_OTP_*` settings. The design is provider-neutral (follows `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` pattern, not `AZURE_*`).</result>

Research and planning for the email OTP feature are done. **Headline discovery: the stated hard prerequisite was never actually shipped** — #725/PR #783 built the rate-limiting infrastructure, but ADR 0035 explicitly deferred the auth-endpoint class, so `otp/request` today would sit in the loose shared `unauth` bucket with no per-email limit at all. The full file:line research digest is posted on umbrella [#738](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/738#issuecomment-5153273633) so it survives this session.

## The plan — ranked by dependency and priority

| # | Task | Issue | Depends on | Complexity → model |
|---|------|-------|-----------|--------------------|
| 1 | Rate-limit `auth` class (middleware, per-IP) | #1127 (half) | nothing | Low — **Sonnet** |
| 2 | Identity migration: `aad_object_id` nullable + unique `lower(email)` + email audit + `/me` nullable fix | #735 | nothing (runs ∥ with 1) | High risk — **Opus** |
| 3 | Backend core: `sessions` + OTP service/mailer + endpoints + seam branch + fail-closed config + per-email counters (#1127's other half) | #734 | 1, 2 **deployed** | Highest — **Opus**, split into 2–3 stacked PRs |
| 4 | Frontend: `otp` mode, two-step sign-in, cookie handling, E2E | #736 | 3's API contract | Medium — **Sonnet** |
| 5 | SMTP pre-flight admin endpoint + runbook | #737 | 3's config block (∥ with 4) | Low — **Sonnet** (Haiku for the docs half) |
| 6 | `/mcp` in OTP-only mode (PAT-only verifier) | #1128 | 3, non-blocking | Medium — **Sonnet** |

Task 2 is the risky one by the ADR's own admission — it touches the identity model every authz decision hangs off, and the risk is real: emails are stored **verbatim from JWT claims** (no normalization), so the duplicate audit must run against prod before the unique index; and `MeResponse.aad_object_id` is non-nullable, meaning an OTP user would 500 on `/me` — a break the migration PR must fix in the same step. Two-step discipline applies: the migration deploys before any code that upserts by email.

**Load-bearing gotchas the research pinned** (all in the umbrella comment with file:line): auth mode is bound at import time, so #734 needs a new `_get_current_user_otp` variant — the existing real-mode function can't serve an OTP-only deployment; the `Security()` ordering trap that caused the #849 PAT leak applies in reverse to cookies; the log scrubber's regex doesn't match `dq_sess_` and must be extended; the session token copies the PAT hash-lookup model (no `compare_digest`) while the 6-digit *code* is what needs the constant-time compare; the `Secure` cookie flag must condition on `X-Forwarded-Proto` or dev over plain HTTP silently drops the cookie; and #1127's per-email counters must live at service level so they stay active when `RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false` (dev/E2E disable the middleware wholesale). One interlock resolved: ADR 0033's `AUTH_OTP_DEFAULT_ROLE` waits for #740 — OTP ships without it, `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` remains the admin axis.

**Two decisions I've made that you may want to veto before implementation starts:**
1. **#1127 split**: middleware `auth` class as its own small PR first; the per-email counters ride inside #734's service PR (they need the parsed/normalized email).
2. **#736 E2E approach**: a Mailhog/smtp4dev container in the CI compose rather than a test-mode code hook — it doesn't weaken prod code paths, which the issue itself asks for.

Per the working agreements, each PR gets the `/code-review` agent flow, migration PRs get the migration-safety reviewer, and everything lands as one-functionality squash-merges with `Fixes #N`. Ready to start executing — say the word and I'll kick off tasks 1 and 2 in parallel.

content.text:
Provide a code review for the given pull request.

To do this, follow these steps precisely:

1. Use a Haiku agent to check if the pull request (a) is closed, (b) is a draft, (c) does not need a code review (eg. because it is an automated pull request, or is very simple and obviously ok), or (d) already has a code review from you from earlier. If so, do not proceed.
2. Use another Haiku agent to give you a list of file paths to (but not the contents of) any relevant CLAUDE.md files from the codebase: the root CLAUDE.md file (if one exists), as well as any CLAUDE.md files in the directories whose files the pull request modified
3. Use a Haiku agent to view the pull request, and ask the agent to return a summary of the change
4. Then, launch 5 parallel Sonnet agents to independently code review the change. The agents should do the following, then return a list of issues and the reason each issue was flagged (eg. CLAUDE.md adherence, bug, historical git context, etc.):
   a. Agent #1: Audit the changes to make sure they compily with the CLAUDE.md. Note that CLAUDE.md is guidance for Claude as it writes code, so not all instructions will be applicable during code review.
   b. Agent #2: Read the file changes in the pull request, then do a shallow scan for obvious bugs. Avoid reading extra context beyond the changes, focusing just on the changes themselves. Focus on large bugs, and avoid small issues and nitpicks. Ignore likely false positives.
   c. Agent #3: Read the git blame and history of the code modified, to identify any bugs in light of that historical context
   d. Agent #4: Read previous pull requests that touched these files, and check for any comments on those pull requests that may also apply to the current pull request.
   e. Agent #5: Read code comments in the modified files, and make sure the changes in the pull request comply with any guidance in the comments.
5. For each issue found in #4, launch a parallel Haiku agent that takes the PR, issue description, and list of CLAUDE.md files (from step 2), and returns a score to indicate the agent's level of confidence for whether the issue is real or false positive. To do that, the agent should score each issue on a scale from 0-100, indicating its level of confidence. For issues that were flagged due to CLAUDE.md instructions, the agent should double check that the CLAUDE.md actually calls out that issue specifically. The scale is (give this rubric to the agent verbatim):
   a. 0: Not confident at all. This is a false positive that doesn't stand up to light scrutiny, or is a pre-existing issue.
   b. 25: Somewhat confident. This might be a real issue, but may also be a false positive. The agent wasn't able to verify that it's a real issue. If the issue is stylistic, it is one that was not explicitly called out in the relevant CLAUDE.md.
   c. 50: Moderately confident. The agent was able to verify this is a real issue, but it might be a nitpick or not happen very often in practice. Relative to the rest of the PR, it's not very important.
   d. 75: Highly confident. The agent double checked the issue, and verified that it is very likely it is a real issue that will be hit in practice. The existing approach in the PR is insufficient. The issue is very important and will directly impact the code's functionality, or it is an issue that is directly mentioned in the relevant CLAUDE.md.
   e. 100: Absolutely certain. The agent double checked the issue, and confirmed that it is definitely a real issue, that will happen frequently in practice. The evidence directly confirms this.
6. Filter out any issues with a score less than 80. If there are no issues that meet this criteria, do not proceed.
7. Use a Haiku agent to repeat the eligibility check from #1, to make sure that the pull request is still eligible for code review.
8. Finally, use the gh bash command to comment back on the pull request with the result. When writing your comment, keep in mind to:
   a. Keep your output brief
   b. Avoid emojis
   c. Link and cite relevant code, files, and URLs

Examples of false positives, for steps 4 and 5:

- Pre-existing issues
- Something that looks like a bug but is not actually a bug
- Pedantic nitpicks that a senior engineer wouldn't call out
- Issues that a linter, typechecker, or compiler would catch (eg. missing or incorrect imports, type errors, broken tests, formatting issues, pedantic style issues like newlines). No need to run these build steps yourself -- it is safe to assume that they will be run separately as part of CI.
- General code quality issues (eg. lack of test coverage, general security issues, poor documentation), unless explicitly required in CLAUDE.md
- Issues that are called out in CLAUDE.md, but explicitly silenced in the code (eg. due to a lint ignore comment)
- Changes in functionality that are likely intentional or are directly related to the broader change
- Real issues, but on lines that the user did not modify in their pull request

Notes:

- Do not check build signal or attempt to build or typecheck the app. These will run separately, and are not relevant to your code review.
- Use `gh` to interact with Github (eg. to fetch a pull request, or to create inline comments), rather than web fetch
- Make a todo list first
- You must cite and link each bug (eg. if referring to a CLAUDE.md, you must link it)
- For your final comment, follow the following format precisely (assuming for this example that you found 3 issues):

---

### Code review

Found 3 issues:

1. <brief description of bug> (CLAUDE.md says "<...>")

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context, note that you MUST provide the full sha and not use bash here, eg. https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/1d54823877c4de72b2316a64032a54afc404e619/README.md#L13-L17>

2. <brief description of bug> (some/other/CLAUDE.md says "<...>")

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context>

3. <brief description of bug> (bug due to <file and code snippet>)

<link to file and line with full sha1 + line range for context>

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)

<sub>- If this code review was useful, please react with 👍. Otherwise, react with 👎.</sub>

---

- Or, if you found no issues:

---

### Code review

No issues found. Checked for bugs and CLAUDE.md compliance.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)

- When linking to code, follow the following format precisely, otherwise the Markdown preview won't render correctly: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-cli-internal/blob/c21d3c10bc8e898b7ac1a2d745bdc9bc4e423afe/package.json#L10-L15
  - Requires full git sha
  - You must provide the full sha. Commands like `https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/$(git rev-parse HEAD)/foo/bar` will not work, since your comment will be directly rendered in Markdown.
  - Repo name must match the repo you're code reviewing
  - # sign after the file name
  - Line range format is L[start]-L[end]
  - Provide at least 1 line of context before and after, centered on the line you are commenting about (eg. if you are commenting about lines 5-6, you should link to `L4-7`)

**PR #1129** adds a fourth rate-limit class (`auth`) for `/api/v1/auth/*` endpoints (OTP mint/verify, ADR 0032). It introduces a **strict per-IP bucket (default 10 req/min) checked BEFORE the bearer branch**, preventing a client from bypassing the auth cap by presenting a token. This is scope item 1 of issue #1127; scope item 2 (per-email OTP counters) ships separately with #734, since the middleware cannot access the parsed request body.

**Head commit SHA:** `d1e99e86842b1d4750ad287f698a783dd0d3fcb1`

| `.env.app.example` | +4, -0 |

- File/line: `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py:71` (`_AUTH_PREFIX`), `:359` (`if path.startswith(_AUTH_PREFIX): return "auth", settings.rate_limit_auth_per_minute, f"ip:{ip}"`); `backend/app/core/config.py:231` (`rate_limit_auth_per_minute: int = 10`) interacting with the unmodified `:251` (`rate_limit_ipv4_prefix: int = Field(default=24, ...)`).

The single global `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX`/`RATE_LIMIT_IPV6_PREFIX` knob can no longer serve both the original "generous limit, defeat NAT-based cap evasion" use case and this new "strict limit, don't collectively punish a shared network" use case simultaneously.

## Findings — PR #1129 (auth rate-limit class), reviewed against rate_limit.py history (#783/#785/#789/#784→#1016)

**1. The new `auth` class inherits the /24 (IPv4) / /64 (IPv6) prefix-folding built for limits ≥120/min, but is capped at 10/min — this collapses to near-total lockout for anyone sharing that prefix, on the one surface where shared-IP traffic is most expected.**

- File/line: `backend/app/core/rate_limit.py:71` (`_AUTH_PREFIX`), `:359` (`if path.startswith(_AUTH_PREFIX): return "auth", settings.rate_limit_auth_per_minute, f"ip:{ip}"`); `backend/app/core/config.py:231` (`rate_limit_auth_per_minute: int = 10`) interacting with the unmodified `:251` (`rate_limit_ipv4_prefix: int = Field(default=24, ...)`).
- Reason flagged, with the historical evidence: #789/#874 (`2d885c2d feat(rate-limit): key per-IP buckets on an address prefix`) added prefix-folding specifically because the *existing* per-IP limits (webhook 120, unauth 120, default `ipall` 1200) were "generous," and the documented trade-off in `config.py` even says so explicitly: *"a prefix that legitimately hosts many independent clients (CGNAT) shares the cap — tune the masks per deployment."* That reasoning assumes a limit large enough that dilution across up to 256 IPv4 hosts (or an entire /64) still leaves headroom. This PR reuses the same global `_bucket_ip()` folding for a bucket capped at **10/min** — one order of magnitude below the smallest existing class. Any legitimate NAT pool (corporate egress, campus network, and especially mobile carrier-grade NAT — the single most common real-world case for an OTP login flow) sharing one /24 now contends for 10 total OTP requests per minute across the whole pool. A modest burst of simultaneous legitimate logins exhausts it and locks out everyone else behind that prefix for the rest of the window.
- This is materially worse than the pre-existing trade-off because: (a) the PR's own docstring/ADR text says the per-email layer (ADR 0032 §8, #734) — the layer that would normally scope abuse to an individual actor rather than a shared network — "lands separately" and isn't in this PR, so the per-IP-prefix bucket is currently the *only* defense on this surface; and (b) none of the three existing per-IP-only classes (`webhook`, `unauth`, and now `auth`) get a config knob to opt out of the shared global prefix width, so tightening it to `/32` to protect OTP traffic would also strip the NAT-evasion protection #789 built for `webhook`/`unauth`. The single global `RATE_LIMIT_IPV4_PREFIX`/`RATE_LIMIT_IPV6_PREFIX` knob can no longer serve both the original "generous limit, defeat NAT-based cap evasion" use case and this new "strict limit, don't collectively punish a shared network" use case simultaneously.
- Not covered by the new tests: both `test_auth_class_429s_separately_from_unauth` and `test_auth_class_not_dodged_by_bearer` (backend/tests/api/test_rate_limiting.py) drive requests from a single fixed test-client IP and never exercise `_bucket_ip`'s prefix-folding for the `auth` class, so this interaction has no regression coverage.

Everything else checked out as sound in light of the history:
- The `auth` class deliberately has **no** `ipall` dual-key ceiling (rate_limit.py's `keys.append(...)` block has no `elif cls == "auth"` branch). This is correct and consistent with #785's rationale: the `ipall` ceiling exists only to close the *multiplicative* bypass created when a class folds a rotating value (token hash for `default`, provider segment for `webhook`) into its primary key — a fresh key per request would otherwise never hit a cap. `auth`'s key is `ip:{ip}` with no folded/rotating component, so it's already single-bucket per IP like `unauth`, and needs no second ceiling.

- No key-namespace collision with `webhook` or `unauth` (`rl:auth:ip:{ip}:{window}` vs `rl:unauth:ip:{ip}:{window}` are distinct Redis keys despite the same `ip:{ip}` key-component), and `_warn_store_unavailable_once`'s `key_kind` domain (`tok`/`ip`) still holds since `auth` keys start with `ip:`.

Code-review comments posted to DataQ PRs must NOT include the reaction-solicitation
footer (`<sub>- If this code review was useful, please react with 👍. Otherwise,
react with 👎.</sub>`), even though the /code-review skill's output template
includes it.

**Why:** user directive 2026-08-01 ("stop adding the … react with 👍/👎 … in PR").
The 🤖 "Generated with Claude Code" attribution line stays; only the reaction
footer is dropped.

**How to apply:** when the code-review flow's final-comment template says to
include the footer, omit that `<sub>` line. Related: [[feedback-review-before-merge]].

I reviewed PR #1131 (diff at head `ab66f303`) against the specific checklist. Findings: **none**.

Verification detail for each checked area:

1. **Migration upgrade/downgrade ordering** (`backend/alembic/versions/7d25617cfaf0_...py`): `downgrade()` runs `SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE aad_object_id IS NULL` and raises `RuntimeError` *before* any `op.drop_index`/`op.alter_column` call when orphans exist. Confirmed by the new migration test `test_downgrade_refuses_instead_of_deleting_otp_users`, which asserts the schema is untouched after the refusal.

2. **Index name consistency**: migration uses `_EMAIL_LOWER_UQ = "uq_users_email_lower"` (line 110, 122, 139); `backend/app/db/models.py` `User.__table_args__` uses the identical literal `"uq_users_email_lower"` (line ~166). Match.

3. **Expression consistency**: migration creates the index with `[sa.text("lower(email)")]` (line 122); the model declares `Index("uq_users_email_lower", text("lower(email)"), unique=True)`. Both are `lower(email)`, not `lower(email::text)` — no drift.

4. **Nullable model change**: `aad_object_id: Mapped[str | None] = mapped_column(String(64), nullable=True, unique=True)` matches the migration's `op.alter_column(..., nullable=True)`; the pre-existing `unique=True` (and thus `uq_users_aad_object_id`) is left untouched by both, consistent with the docstring's claim that NULLs stay distinct under a unique constraint in Postgres.

5. **`MeResponse` change**: `aad_object_id: str | None` in `backend/app/api/v1/me.py` mirrors the now-nullable model column; `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)` is unaffected.

6. **`frontend/src/api/me.ts`**: `aad_object_id: string | null` matches the backend contract; grep confirms no other frontend code currently reads this field, consistent with the added comment.

7. **Fixture de-duplication risk**: checked every touched test file (`test_checks.py`, `test_nul_rejection.py`, `test_orchestration_events*.py`, `test_schedules.py`, `test_suites.py`, `test_trigger_bindings.py`, `test_connection_service.py`, `test_orchestration_service.py`, `test_poll_targeting.py`, `test_polling.py`) for any assertion keyed on the literal email string produced by the changed helpers (`owner@example.com`, `dev@example.com`, etc.). None found — the helpers' email values are never asserted on, only used to satisfy the FK/ownership relationship. The change is also load-bearing rather than cosmetic: `test_suites.py`'s `test_list_filters_by_connection` calls `_connection(db_session)` twice in one test, which previously would have inserted two `User` rows both with the literal `"owner@example.com"` — a real collision under the new `uq_users_email_lower` index that the randomized suffix fixes.

No other issues surfaced in the changed hunks (`docs/architecture.md` ER-diagram annotations are documentation-only and match the schema change).

## PR #1131 (7d25617cfaf0) — Migration-Safety Audit

### 1. Does running code INSERT into `users` without `aad_object_id`, or break when the column allows NULL?

**No risk.** Read-only audit of `origin/main` found exactly two write paths into `users`, both funneling through the same helper:

- `backend/app/core/auth.py::_upsert_user` (lines ~140–162) — called from `_get_current_user_real` (AAD claim `oid`, always present) and `_get_current_user_dev_bypass` (`DEV_BYPASS_AAD_OID`, a fixed constant).
- `backend/app/mcp/auth.py::resolve_current_user` — calls the *same* `_upsert_user`, with `aad_oid = claims.get("oid")` guarded by `if aad_oid:` before the call, and dev-bypass uses the same fixed constant.
- `backend/scripts/seed_dev.py` also goes through `_upsert_user` with `DEV_BYPASS_AAD_OID`.
- `backend/app/services/user_service.py` is read-only (search only).

No path constructs a `User` with `aad_object_id=None`. Widening the column to nullable is purely additive from the perspective of every currently-deployed writer — **acceptable by design**, this is exactly the two-step migration discipline CLAUDE.md §6/§10 calls for (schema first, `#734`'s email-linking code ships separately).

`backend/app/api/v1/me.py`'s `MeResponse.aad_object_id` was correctly widened to `str | None` in the same PR — necessary because `response_model` validation is strict and would otherwise 500 once a NULL-aad row exists, but no such row exists yet, so this is inert until `#734` ships.

### 2. Can the new `uq_users_email_lower` index break an EXISTING write path? — **Real, currently-unmitigated risk**

This is real, not "acceptable by design" under ADR 0032 decision 6. Decision 6 covers the **future** state (`#734`, OTP↔AAD email linking) — it says nothing about two distinct AAD identities colliding on email, and it doesn't ship in this PR.

**Failure scenario:** Today, `_upsert_user` (`backend/app/core/auth.py:140-162`) does `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (aad_object_id) DO UPDATE`. If Azure AD ever sends the same (case-insensitive) email for two *different* `oid` values — e.g., a mailbox reissued to a new employee after the previous owner leaves, a guest invite reusing an external address already tied to another account, or a legitimate case-drift on a *different* physical account than the one that first registered that casing — today both succeed as two separate `users` rows. After this migration, the second user's login hits `uq_users_email_lower` on either the `INSERT` or the `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET email=...` branch (a same-oid claim's email change can also collide with an *unrelated* row's already-registered normalized email). SQLAlchemy raises `IntegrityError`, uncaught in `_upsert_user`, propagates through `get_current_user` → FastAPI's catch-all `Exception` handler (`backend/app/core/errors.py::_unhandled_exception_handler`) → a bare `500 internal_error`. Same code path is shared by `backend/app/mcp/auth.py::resolve_current_user`, so `/mcp` auth fails the same way.

This is not data corruption (session rollback via `get_db`'s `except Exception: db.rollback()` is clean, transaction-scoped), but it **blocks that user's login/every request** with an opaque 500 instead of a clean 4xx — the exact class of bug CLAUDE.md's go-live section calls out (the NUL-byte-500 precedent, #567/#570).

Notably, this is **inconsistent with the codebase's own established convention**: `connection_service.py`, `share_service.py`, `trigger_binding_service.py`, and `check_service.py` all catch `IntegrityError` from unique-constraint races and translate them into clean `DataQError` 409/422s. `_upsert_user` — the one identity write path, and the one this PR adds a new unique constraint against — does not follow that pattern.

**Severity/likelihood:** low probability today (prod has ~6 demo AAD users with distinct emails per current state), but the exposure window is open-ended — it lasts from this migration's deploy until `#734` ships the linking logic, not just the deploy instant, and nothing in this PR documents or mitigates it (the migration's own "MANDATORY PRE-DEPLOY" audit covers only *pre-existing* duplicate rows at index-creation time, not *new* collisions written by the old, unchanged `_upsert_user` afterward).

**Recommendation:** file a GitHub issue (per CLAUDE.md "every finding ends fixed or filed") tracking that `_upsert_user` needs an `IntegrityError` → clean `DataQError` translation on `uq_users_email_lower`, ideally landing no later than `#734` alongside the linking logic it's the natural home for.

### 3. Migration transaction / locks — **no issue, confirmed safe for current scale**

- `alembic/env.py` sets `transaction_per_migration=True`; both DDL statements run in one transaction, consistent with the precedent revision (`1a2b3c4d5e6f`).
- `op.alter_column(..., nullable=True)` (DROP NOT NULL) is metadata-only in Postgres — no table rewrite, near-instant, briefly ACCESS EXCLUSIVE.
- `op.create_index(..., unique=True)` with **no `CONCURRENTLY`** takes a SHARE lock, blocking concurrent writers (every authenticated AAD request calls `_upsert_user`, which is a write) for the index-build duration. Correctly *not* using `CONCURRENTLY`, since that cannot run inside a transaction block anyway and cannot report the duplicate-email conflict as a clean transactional abort (the migration's own stated rationale). Given the documented table size ("tens of rows in the largest deployment we know of"), this is sub-second — verified reasonable for current/foreseeable single-tenant scale. No `CONCURRENTLY` needed.

### 4. Downgrade refusal — **verified clean, cannot leave a half-applied state**

`downgrade()` (lines 125–140) runs the `SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE aad_object_id IS NULL` check **before any DDL** and raises `RuntimeError` immediately if `orphans > 0`, touching nothing. Two layers of protection:
1. The explicit pre-check makes the common case a clean, actionable no-op.
2. Even in a TOCTOU race (a NULL-aad row inserted by a concurrent session between the check and the `ALTER COLUMN ... NOT NULL`), the resulting Postgres error (`column contains null values`) would abort mid-DDL — but `transaction_per_migration=True` rolls the whole transaction back regardless, so the schema is never left partially downgraded (index dropped but column still nullable, or vice versa) either way.

No half-applied-state risk found.

### Summary

| # | Area | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | NULL-aad INSERT from running code | No risk — no writer inserts NULL; purely additive |
| 2 | New `lower(email)` unique index vs. existing write path | **Real deploy-window risk** — uncaught `IntegrityError` → bare 500 on a same-email/different-oid collision, inconsistent with the codebase's own IntegrityError-handling convention elsewhere; recommend filing an issue against `_upsert_user` |
| 3 | Lock/transaction concerns | No issue — plain `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` sub-second on a tiny table, correctly avoids `CONCURRENTLY` inside the transaction |
| 4 | Downgrade half-applied state | No issue — pre-DDL check + transactional wrapping both guarantee clean abort |

Files reviewed: `backend/alembic/versions/7d25617cfaf0_users_nullable_aad_unique_lower_email.py`, `backend/app/db/models.py` (User), `backend/app/api/v1/me.py`, `backend/app/core/auth.py`, `backend/app/mcp/auth.py`, `backend/app/services/user_service.py`, `backend/scripts/seed_dev.py`, `backend/app/core/errors.py`, `backend/app/db/session.py`, `backend/alembic/env.py`, `docs/adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md` — all read at `origin/main` / PR diff via `gh pr diff 1131`, no working-tree mutation.

## Findings

**1. Migration's lock-note mischaracterizes the lock class as SHARE when the transaction actually holds ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for its full duration — the exact mechanism of the #748 production incident.**

- **File/line:** `backend/alembic/versions/7d25617cfaf0_users_nullable_aad_unique_lower_email.py:49-51` (docstring "Lock note"), and the `upgrade()` body at lines 114-116 (`op.alter_column(..., nullable=True)` immediately followed by `op.create_index(...)`, both in one `transaction_per_migration=True` transaction).
- **Derives from:** the 2026-07-10 migration-lock incident, [#748](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/748) ("a queued ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on `connections` blocked every new reader for ~25 minutes"), and its follow-up [#1043](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1043) ("So a revision can set `transactional_ddl = False` and use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`... the only options on a hot table are 'take a write-blocking lock' or 'skip the index' — the same incident, self-inflicted"). The reasoning this migration's docstring uses ("plain `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX`... the SHARE lock is sub-second") is copied near-verbatim from the precedent it cites, `1a2b3c4d5e6f_lineage_edges_nullable_connection.py` (PR [#776](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/776), lines 23-27: "plain CREATE INDEX takes a SHARE lock blocking writes for the build").
- **The problem:** Postgres locks are held until COMMIT and only escalate within a transaction, never downgrade. `op.alter_column(..., nullable=True)` (an `ALTER TABLE ... DROP NOT NULL`) takes `AccessExclusiveLock` — I verified this empirically against real Postgres (two `docker exec` sessions: a transaction holding `BEGIN; ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN aad_object_id DROP NOT NULL;` open, `pg_locks` showed `AccessExclusiveLock | granted=t`, and a concurrent `SELECT * FROM users` in a second session hung and hit its `statement_timeout`). Because the `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` runs in the *same* transaction right after, the already-held `AccessExclusiveLock` persists through the index build and until commit — it is never merely a `SHARE` lock. `AccessExclusiveLock` blocks **all reads**, not just writes, which is precisely the #748 failure mode (readers hang, `/healthz` stays green).
- **Failure scenario:** `users` is touched on essentially every authenticated request — `_upsert_user` in `backend/app/core/auth.py:139-165` runs an `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` against `users` on every non-PAT bearer request, and most authz/ownership checks join against `users.id`/`created_by`. If this migration's `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` build (or the wait to acquire the lock, per `env.py`'s 15s `lock_timeout`) takes any non-trivial time during a deploy under real traffic, every `/me` call and every request that upserts or reads `users` blocks for that whole window — a smaller-scale repeat of #748, on a table read/written far more universally than `connections` or `lineage_edges` (the precedent's target, which has a narrower read pattern).
- **Why it's worth fixing despite the "tens of rows" argument:** the row-count argument bounds index-*build* time, not lock-*acquisition* wait time, and it doesn't change the lock *class* — the docstring's safety claim is about the wrong lock, which could mislead a future migration author copying this pattern onto a bigger or hotter table. Given #1043 built `autocommit_block()`/`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` tooling specifically so hot-table indexes don't have to take this risk, and `users` is arguably hotter than either prior use of this pattern, the migration should either use that tooling here, or the docstring should honestly describe the lock as ACCESS EXCLUSIVE spanning both statements and justify acceptance on duration/table-size grounds rather than mischaracterizing it as SHARE.
- **Severity:** should-fix, not blocking — practical impact is likely sub-second given the real row count, and `env.py`'s `lock_timeout=15s` (landed in #927 specifically to address #748) ensures the migration fails fast rather than queueing indefinitely if it can't get the lock. But the finding is real (verified live) and the documented reasoning is factually wrong in a way that matters for the next person who copies this file as a template — which is exactly what happened once already (this PR copying `1a2b3c4d5e6f`'s already-inaccurate note).

**No other findings survived verification:**
- Revision-id collision (the twice-bitten class per memory/#1042 and #1043-era history): checked — `7d25617cfaf0` is unique across all 42 migration files, `70a054d4c469` has exactly one child, and `alembic heads` against a live scratch DB shows a single head. Clean.
- ApiKey unique-INDEX-not-constraint precedent (`models.py:167-175`, from the #990/#1004 parity work): the new `User.__table_args__` index name (`uq_users_email_lower`) is explicitly kept identical between the model and the migration, with a comment citing that exact precedent. Ran the actual parity test (`backend/tests/db/test_migration_parity.py`) against live Postgres — passes. No code anywhere keys off this constraint/index name in error handling (only `connection_service._conflict_from_integrity_error` does that pattern, and it targets a different index). Verified benign.
- All 15 new/changed tests (`test_user_identity.py`, `test_users_identity_migration.py`, `test_me.py`) pass against real Postgres in an isolated scratch DB I created and dropped for this review.
- No reader in `backend/app` besides the fixed `me.py` assumes `User.aad_object_id` is non-null.

Based on my verification of the code, I can confirm the finding is substantive:

## Verification Summary

**Schema Change (PR #1131):**
- Adds `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_users_email_lower ON users (lower(email))`
- Makes `aad_object_id` nullable to support OTP sign-in (ADR 0032)

**Code Reality:**
The unchanged `_upsert_user()` (lines 139–168 in auth.py) does:
```python
insert(User).on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["aad_object_id"], ...)
```
This handles conflicts **only on `aad_object_id`**, not on the new `uq_users_email_lower` index.

**Collision Scenarios:**
1. **New AAD identity with case-variant email:** A user with oid="aaaa" and email="john@example.com" exists. A different user (oid="bbbb") signs in with email="John@Example.com". The INSERT proceeds (oid is new) but violates the unique email index → **unhandled IntegrityError**.
2. **Same identity email claim change:** A user (oid="aaaa") previously had email="john@example.com". Their JWT now claims email="John@Example.com". The UPDATE half of ON CONFLICT fires but violates the index if another row holds that email → **unhandled IntegrityError**.

**Working Agreement Violation:**
CONTRIBUTING.md rule 32 explicitly states: "catch the `IntegrityError` to surface a **409**... not an unhandled 500." Other services (connection_service, share_service, trigger_binding_service) correctly catch and translate IntegrityError; auth.py does not.

**Test Coverage:**
- The PR adds `test_email_uniqueness_is_case_insensitive()` which directly tests that email collisions raise IntegrityError
- All test fixtures were updated to randomize emails (adding UUID suffixes), indicating awareness of this issue
- Zero tests for `_upsert_user` itself — the collision path is untested at the auth layer

**Realism in Single-Tenant AAD:**
- Email re-issuance when employees leave is a real scenario (old cached tokens + new employee = same email)
- The schema's design explicitly accounts for collisions, suggesting developers expected them

---

**Score: 75**

**Justification:** This is a highly confident, real issue that violates an explicit CONTRIBUTING.md rule (mandate to catch IntegrityError, not surface 500). The collision precondition is plausible in single-tenant AAD with email re-issuance cycles, the schema was deliberately designed to enforce it, and every occurrence blocks login entirely on both web and MCP endpoints. While not the most frequent error, when it occurs it's a complete auth failure for that user until resolved. The fix is straightforward (catch IntegrityError → raise DataQError 409), matching established patterns elsewhere in the codebase.

The diagnosis was wrong too — each site had TWO markers, one on the flagged node (load-bearing) and one outside its range (inert), and the `no failed test` warning names the inert one without saying which is which.
